source.title: Protocols for Observational Studies: Methods and Open Problems

accepted.question_text: For people who play American football, what amount of playing imposes substantial health risks, including brain-damage concerns such as chronic traumatic encephalopathy and later-life mental-health or cognitive problems, and what rule changes could reduce those risks while preserving the benefits of playing football?
accepted.context_brief: American football exposure and safety rules

evidence.quote: “The Scars From ‘Bell-Ringing’ Football Tackles” (editorial, 7/29) highlights a high rate of CTE [the type of brain damage football is hypothesized to cause] among former football players who donated their brains for study, and suggests safety concerns about not only pro but also high school football.
However, our research in JAMA Neurology finds among 1950s high school graduates, football players don’t have higher rates of later-life depression or impaired cognition than non-football players.

Many people love playing football and playing promotes physical fitness, teamwork and recreation. More research is needed into what amount of playing imposes substantial risks and what rule changes could reduce risks.

accepted.question_text: In matched observational studies, when researchers must decide whether to specify the study protocol before or after matching treated and control units, what methods besides prespecifying important matching covariates before matching can reduce researcher hope bias, where researcher hope bias means understating uncertainty or declining to match on possible confounders because the researcher hopes the matched study will retain enough power to be informative?

evidence.quote: For specifying before vs. after the match, the potential of researcher hope bias (understatement of uncertainty from specifying a protocol after matching because the researcher hopes it will be feasible to learn something useful from the data) needs to be traded off against the information one can learn about unmeasured confounding from specifying a protocol after matching.

One potential way to reduce researcher hope bias is to before matching, specify the list of covariates that are thought to be important to match on and provide reasons in the final protocol for any changes from this initial list [15]. It would be useful if future work could provide other ways of reducing researcher hope bias.

accepted.question_text: In an observational study that uses an elaborate theory, meaning a prespecified set of multiple predictions about how the data should look if the treatment has an effect, what methods can assess the evidence for the elaborate theory when investigators may want both prioritized testing of some predictions and information about all aspects of the theory, including the fraction of the theory corroborated and the evidence for individual aspects?

evidence.quote: An elaborate theory is a set of multiple predictions about how the data would look if the treatment has an effect.
Thus, an elaborate theory and a plan to test it should be specified in the protocol.

Although ordered testing of an elaborate theory has considerable advantages, one negative aspect is that although one might want to put a higher priority on certain aspects of the theory, one might want some information on all aspects. A different approach to assessing the evidence for an elaborate theory is to make inferences about the fraction of the elaborate theory that is corroborated as well as individual aspects of the theory [65]. Further research on ways to assess the evidence for an elaborate theory would be useful.

accepted.question_text: For sample-splitting methods in observational study protocols, where data are randomly divided into a planning sample used to choose hypotheses, outcomes, or subgroups and an analysis sample used for confirmatory testing with appropriate multiplicity correction, how should researchers choose a good fraction of the data to allocate to the planning sample as a function of the total sample size?

evidence.quote: Examples of methods that control for the familywise multiple testing error rate are Bonferroni-Holm [56] or splitting in which the data is randomly divided into a planning sample and an analysis sample, hypotheses are chosen to test based on examining the planning sample and then the chosen hypotheses are tested on the analysis sample using Bonferroni-Holm with the number of hypotheses now being the number of chosen hypotheses from the planning sample [25, 117, 47].

In Section 5, we demonstrated that splitting may be a useful approach for selecting outcomes and subgroups in an observational study. Some problems that have not been well explored for the approach include (i) what is a good fraction for the planning sample based on the sample size?; (ii) how should we decide how many and which outcomes should be carried forward from the planning sample to test in the analysis sample?; and (iii) instead of just having one planning sample and one analysis sample, how can we use sequential analysis methods to allow for multiple possible planning samples before deciding on an analysis sample?

accepted.question_text: For sample-splitting methods in observational study protocols, where a planning sample is used to choose candidate outcomes and a separate analysis sample is used for confirmatory testing, how should researchers decide how many outcomes and which outcomes should be carried forward from the planning sample to be tested in the analysis sample?

accepted.question_text: How should observational-study authors summarize conclusions when the prespecified primary analysis is not statistically significant but a secondary analysis is statistically significant and a post hoc explanation makes the secondary finding appear consistent with a true treatment effect, so that the summary does not give excessive weight to the secondary result or selectively interpret the findings?
accepted.context_brief: Reporting secondary findings after null primary analysis

evidence.quote: In the mountaintop mining study, the primary analysis yielded insignificant results but an aspect of the secondary analysis yielded significant results and we thought of a post hoc explanation for why this pattern could be consistent with a true treatment effect. How do we best summarize the conclusions of a study in this common situation?

In this conclusion, did we pay too much heed to a secondary analysis finding? Did we selectively interpret the findings? It would be useful to have more empirical research on how readers interpret language in abstracts and conclusions of papers.

accepted.question_text: What empirical evidence is needed about how readers interpret language in abstracts and conclusions, especially when observational studies report nonsignificant primary analyses together with significant secondary analyses, so that reporting guidance can reduce selective interpretation of study findings?
accepted.context_brief: Reader interpretation of abstracts and conclusions

evidence.quote: In this conclusion, did we pay too much heed to a secondary analysis finding? Did we selectively interpret the findings? It would be useful to have more empirical research on how readers interpret language in abstracts and conclusions of papers.

accepted.question_text: Can selective interpretation in observational studies be reduced by having the protocol prewrite result-contingent discussions and conclusions for the different findings that might occur, and how should such a protocol handle the difficulty of thinking insightfully about hypothetical results and the extra time required?

evidence.quote: An extreme remedy for selective interpretation would be to, in the protocol, write the paper with blanks for the results and different discussions/conclusions that would be presented based on what the results are (like writing a Choose Your Own Adventure book [83]). Potential problems with this approach include that it might be harder to think insightfully about results that hypothetically could occur vs. those that did occur and it is time consuming. Nevertheless the approach may be worth trying.
